Propensity Score Weighting Using BART

Source: R/weightit2bart.R
method_bart.Rd

This page explains the details of estimating weights from Bayesian additive regression trees (BART)-based propensity scores by setting method = "bart" in the call to weightit() or weightitMSM(). This method can be used with binary, multi-category, and continuous treatments, as well as for estimating censoring weights.

In general, this method relies on estimating propensity scores using BART and then converting those propensity scores into weights using a formula that depends on the desired estimand. This method relies on bartisan::bartisan() from the bartisan package, which fits BART models with soft decision rules and with likelihoods beyond the normal using the sampler of Linero (2025).

Binary Treatments

For binary treatments, this method estimates the propensity scores using bartisan::bartisan() with a binomial likelihood, by default with a logit link (see link in Additional Arguments below). The following estimands are allowed: ATE, ATT, ATC, ATO, ATM, and ATOS. Weights can also be computed using marginal mean weighting through stratification for the ATE, ATT, and ATC. See get_w_from_ps() for details.

Multi-Category Treatments

For multi-category treatments, the propensity scores are estimated using a single call to bartisan::bartisan() with a multinomial likelihood (bartisan::multinomial() ), by default with a logit link (see link in Additional Arguments below). One forest is fit for each treatment level, and the predicted probabilities for each unit sum to 1. The following estimands are allowed: ATE, ATT, ATC, ATO, and ATM. The weights for each estimand are computed using the standard formulas. Weights can also be computed using marginal mean weighting through stratification for the ATE, ATT, and ATC. See get_w_from_ps() for details.

Continuous Treatments

For continuous treatments, weights are estimated as \(w_i = f_A(a_i) / f_{A|X}(a_i)\), where \(f_A(a_i)\) (known as the stabilization factor) is the unconditional density of treatment evaluated at the observed treatment value and \(f_{A|X}(a_i)\) (known as the generalized propensity score) is the conditional density of treatment given the covariates evaluated at the observed treatment value. The conditional density is estimated directly by a BART model for the treatment whose form is set by the family argument (see Additional Arguments below). By default, this is bartisan::dpm() , a model whose mean is a sum of trees and whose error distribution is a Dirichlet process mixture of normals estimated from the data (George et al., 2019), so no parametric form for the density needs to be assumed. The error distribution is the same for all units, though, so when the variance of the treatment may depend on the covariates, a different family may be preferable, such as family = "gaussian_ls", which fits a normal model in which both the mean and the logarithm of the standard deviation are sums of trees. \(f_A(.)\) is estimated by marginalizing over \(f_{A|X}(.)\).

Multilevel Treatment Models

When the model formula contains lme4-style random intercept terms (e.g., treat ~ x1 + x2 + (1 | school)), the random intercepts are included in the BART model directly; see Random Intercepts at bartisan::bartisan() . This can improve balance when units are clustered (e.g., patients within hospitals or students within schools). Multiple grouping factors (e.g., (1 | school) + (1 | district)) and nesting ((1 | district/school)) are allowed, but random slopes are not; a variable whose effect varies by group belongs in the fixed part of the formula, where a tree can split on it and on the group together. The grouping variables are taken from data. The estimated propensity scores (or conditional densities for continuous treatments) include the estimated random effects; i.e., they are cluster-specific.

Censoring Weights

For censoring weights, requested by wrapping the censoring indicator in .cens(), a single BART model of the probability of being censored is fit, and the weights are 1/P(C = 0 | X) for the units still under observation and 0 for the censored units. The returned propensity score is the probability of being censored.

Longitudinal Treatments

For longitudinal treatments, the weights are the product of the weights estimated at each time point.

Sampling Weights

Sampling weights are supported through s.weights, except with the default family for continuous treatments. Before being supplied to bartisan::bartisan() as prior weights, they are scaled to have a mean of 1 among the units in the model, so that the fit does not depend on their scale. For continuous treatments, they are also used in computing the marginal density of the treatment in the numerator of the weights. The default family for continuous treatments, bartisan::dpm() , does not accept prior weights, so supplying sampling weights that vary across units with it is an error. To use sampling weights with a continuous treatment, supply a family that accepts them, such as family = gaussian() or family = "gaussian_ls".

Missing Data

In the presence of missing data, the following value(s) for missing are allowed:

"mia" (default)

The missing values are left in the covariates and handled by the trees themselves using missingness incorporated in attributes; see Missing Predictor Values at bartisan::bartisan() . Each splitting rule on a covariate with missing values also determines which side of the split the units missing that covariate go to, or splits on whether the covariate is missing at all, and these choices are made by the sampler along with the rest of the tree. The estimated propensity scores are then conditional on the observed covariate values and on which covariates are missing. With use.offset = TRUE, the generalized linear model that supplies the offset uses missingness indicators as described for "ind" below. The covariates output in the resulting weightit object will be the original covariates with the NAs.

"ind"

First, for each variable with missingness, a new missingness indicator variable is created which takes the value 1 if the original covariate is NA and 0 otherwise. The missingness indicators are added to the model formula as main effects. The missing values in the covariates are then replaced with the covariate medians. For a categorical covariate, the missing values are instead given a category of their own. The weight estimation then proceeds with this new formula and set of covariates. The covariates output in the resulting weightit object will be the original covariates with the NAs.

M-estimation

M-estimation is not supported.

Details

BART works by fitting a sum-of-trees model for the treatment or probability of treatment. The number of trees is determined by the num_trees argument. Bayesian priors are used for the hyperparameters, so the result is a posterior distribution of predicted values for each unit. The mean of these for each unit is taken for use in computing the (generalized) propensity score. Although the hyperparameters governing the priors can be modified by supplying arguments to weightit() that are passed to the BART fitting function, the default values tend to work well and require little modification. Unlike many other machine learning methods, no loss function is optimized and the hyperparameters do not need to be tuned (e.g., using cross-validation), though performance can benefit from tuning. BART tends to balance sparseness with flexibility by using very weak learners as the trees, which makes it suitable for capturing complex functions without specifying a particular functional form and without overfitting.

The covariates are supplied to bartisan::bartisan() as they appear in the model formula rather than as a model matrix, so a categorical covariate remains a single variable whose levels a tree can split into any two groups (see categorical at bartisan::bartisan_control() ). Transformed terms (e.g., I(x^2)) are included as given, and an interaction term is represented by its component variables, since the trees can find interactions among them without one being specified.

By default, the decision rules in each tree are soft, as in the SoftBart model of Linero and Yang (2018): an observation reaches every leaf with some weight, so the fitted propensity score is a smooth function of the covariates rather than a step function. Smoother propensity scores tend to be better calibrated and to yield less extreme weights than those from standard BART. Soft rules are slower than hard rules; the standard BART sampler can be requested with gate = "hard". See bartisan::bartisan_control() for details.

Reproducibility

BART has a random component. bartisan uses R's random number generator, so calling set.seed() before weightit() makes the results reproducible, including when the chains run in parallel, since each chain is given its own random number stream. The seed argument accepted by earlier versions of this method, which used dbarts, is ignored with a warning.

Parallel Processing

When chains is greater than 1 and the future.apply package is installed, the chains run in parallel under whatever future::plan() has been set. See Parallelization with future at bartisan::bartisan_control() .

Additional Arguments

All arguments to bartisan::bartisan_control() can be passed through weightit() or weightitMSM() to control the sampler and the priors, including num_trees, num_draws, num_burn, chains, gate, and sparsity. Their defaults are those of bartisan_control(). For compatibility with earlier versions of this method, which used dbarts, the following arguments are translated to their bartisan_control() equivalents when supplied: n.trees to num_trees, n.samples to num_draws, n.burn to num_burn, and n.chains to chains. A natively named argument takes precedence over its translation. n.threads is ignored (see Parallel Processing below), and seed is ignored with a warning (see Reproducibility below).

For binary and multi-category treatments and for censoring weights, only the link of the model described above can be changed, using link; family is ignored. For continuous treatments, the model is set by family, described below.

The following additional arguments may be supplied:

use.offset

logical; whether to use the linear predictor resulting from a generalized linear model as an offset to the BART model. If TRUE, this fits a binomial regression model with the link specified by link (for binary treatments) or a linear regression model (for continuous treatments) and supplies the linear predictor to the offset argument of bartisan(), overriding any supplied argument to offset. With missing = "mia", this model uses missingness indicators for the covariates with missing values. Default is FALSE to omit this offset. Only allowed for binary and continuous treatments.

For binary and multi-category treatments, the following arguments may be supplied:

link

for binary treatments and censoring weights, the link function of the binomial model. Allowable options include "logit" (the default), "probit", and "cloglog". For multi-category treatments, the link function of the multinomial model, which can be "logit" (the default) or "probit"; with "probit", the probabilities have no closed form and are computed by simulation (see bartisan::multinomial() ).

subclass

integer; the number of subclasses to use for computing weights using marginal mean weighting through stratification (MMWS). If NULL, standard inverse probability weights (and their extensions) will be computed; if a number greater than 1, subclasses will be formed and weights will be computed based on subclass membership. See get_w_from_ps() for details and references.

For continuous treatments, the following arguments may be supplied:

family

the model for the conditional density of the treatment, given as a family object or the name of one; see bartisan-families. Default is bartisan::dpm() , which estimates the shape of the error distribution from the data but does not accept sampling weights. Other options include bartisan::gaussian_ls() for a normal density whose mean and standard deviation both depend on the covariates and gaussian() for a normal density with a single standard deviation; both accept sampling weights. gaussian_ls() can capture a variance that differs across units but takes several times as long to fit as dpm(), and, like gaussian(), it assumes the conditional density is normal, which can yield extreme weights when the treatment is skewed. With family = "ordinal" (bartisan::ordinal() ), each observed value of the treatment is a category of an ordinal model, and the weights are the ratio of the proportion of units with each unit's treatment value (weighted by the sampling weights) to the probability of that value given the covariates, as for a discrete treatment.

The density, bw, adjust, kernel, and n arguments that other methods use to specify the conditional density are not used by this method and are ignored with a warning, since the density is estimated by the model specified by family.

Additional Outputs

obj

When include.obj = TRUE, the bartisan_fit object used to generate the predicted values. For multi-category treatments, this is a single fit, since one multinomial model is fit for all treatment levels. The predicted probabilities used to compute the propensity scores can be extracted using bartisan::predict.bartisan_fit() with type = "prob", and the conditional density of a continuous treatment with type = "density".

References

Chipman, H. A., George, E. I., & McCulloch, R. E. (2010). BART: Bayesian additive regression trees. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 4(1), 266–298. doi:10.1214/09-AOAS285

Hill, J., Weiss, C., & Zhai, F. (2011). Challenges With Propensity Score Strategies in a High-Dimensional Setting and a Potential Alternative. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 46(3), 477–513. doi:10.1080/00273171.2011.570161

Linero, A. R. (2025). Generalized Bayesian additive regression trees models: beyond conditional conjugacy. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 120(549), 356–369. doi:10.1080/01621459.2024.2337156

Linero, A. R., & Yang, Y. (2018). Bayesian regression tree ensembles that adapt to smoothness and sparsity. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 80(5), 1087–1110. doi:10.1111/rssb.12293

  • Continuous treatments

George, E., Laud, P., Logan, B., McCulloch, R., & Sparapani, R. (2019). Fully Nonparametric Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. In Topics in Identification, Limited Dependent Variables, Partial Observability, Experimentation, and Flexible Modeling: Part B (Advances in Econometrics, Vol. 40B, pp. 89–110). Emerald Publishing Limited. doi:10.1108/S0731-90532019000040B006

Note that many references that deal with BART for causal inference focus on estimating potential outcomes with BART, not the propensity scores, and so are not directly relevant when using BART to estimate propensity scores for weights.

See method_glm for additional references on propensity score weighting more generally.

See also

weightit(), weightitMSM(), get_w_from_ps()

method_super for stacking predictions from several machine learning methods, including BART.

vignette("weighting-methods") for descriptions of all the weighting methods and guidance on choosing among them.

Examples

data("lalonde", package = "cobalt")

set.seed(123)

#Balancing covariates between treatment groups (binary)
(W1 <- weightit(treat ~ age + educ + married +
                  nodegree + re74, data = lalonde,
                method = "bart", estimand = "ATT"))
#> A weightit object
#>  - method: "bart" (propensity score weighting with BART)
#>  - number of obs.: 614
#>  - sampling weights: none
#>  - treatment: 2-category
#>  - estimand: ATT (focal: 1)
#>  - covariates: age, educ, married, nodegree, re74

summary(W1)
#>                   Summary of weights
#>

#>  Control 3.239 3.39 3.56 4.387 11.793

#> ─ Weight statistics:

#> 
#>            Control Treated

cobalt::bal.tab(W1)
